title: Vaisakhi: 1699, 1919 and today
hookLine: one day that holds the Khalsa's birth, a massacre, and a harvest

cards: Three scenes, one day. In the fields, wheat falls to the sickle. In the gurdwaras, Sikhs sing the birthday of the Khalsa.
And in Amritsar, some people stand quietly in a walled garden. Guru Nanak has a line in the Asa di Var that sounds strange on a festival: suffering became the medicine, and comfort the disease.
Vaisakhi is a day that can hold it. Today's title carries two years and a word: the year tradition gives for the Khalsa's birth, the year of the garden, and today.

teach.b: This path has spent whole days on each of these. Today, hold them in one hand. First, birth.
At Anandpur, on Vaisakhi, Guru Gobind Singh called for those who would give their heads, and the five beloved stood up. The amrit was stirred, and the Khalsa was born.
That's the first year in the title, the date tradition gives.
Then grief. On a Vaisakhi much later, troops fired on an unarmed gathering in Jallianwala Bagh, the garden this path stood in a week ago. That's the second year.
Then harvest. Long before either, Vaisakhi was the harvest day in Punjab, and tradition says Guru Amar Das asked the Sikhs to gather at Vaisakhi.
The harvest comes every year, whatever else happened. That's the last word in the title: today. Why can one day hold all three?
On Ang 469, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that suffering became the medicine and comfort the disease, because when there is comfort, the One is forgotten. He isn't praising pain.
On one reading, hardship can keep the One in mind, where comfort lets the One slip away.

So on Vaisakhi, the harvest and the birth are celebrated fully, and the grief is not pushed out of the room. Joy without memory would forget the garden. Memory without joy would forget the Khalsa's birthday and the wheat.
The same day holds kirtan, langar, processions, and, in Amritsar, silence in a garden.

how: On Vaisakhi, Sikhs gather in gurdwaras for kirtan and Ardas, celebrate the founding of the Khalsa with nagar kirtan processions and langar, and in Punjab mark the wheat harvest. In Amritsar, people also visit the Jallianwala Bagh memorial.

o: the winter day when the torn paper is remembered
the spring day of harvest, the Khalsa's birth and memory
a day of fasting kept before the monsoon

games.q: one day, three memories — tap the pairs.

s: Vaisakhi became a gathering day only with the Khalsa
it was already the harvest day, and tradition says Guru Amar Das asked the Sikhs to gather then.
in Ang 469, Guru Nanak is praising pain
he says that when there is comfort, the One is forgotten. on one reading, hardship keeps the One in mind.
the harvest is part of Vaisakhi whatever else the year held
the wheat comes in every year, whatever else happened.

games.q: a friend says Vaisakhi is just a harvest holiday. what does today's lesson add?
o: it also holds the Khalsa's birth and the grief of the garden.
it's only about the Khalsa now.
games.why: one day holds three: birth, grief and harvest. Guru Nanak's line on Ang 469 is one way to hear how grief can sit inside a festival without ruling it.

practice: On the first long breath, bring to mind something newly born in your life, a friendship, a habit, an idea, and give thanks for it; on the next, something you've lost, not to reopen it, but to give thanks that you were able to love it.
On the third, give thanks for something ready, a harvest: work finished, a season you came through. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after each one, then rest with all three.

wordCard.voice: Vaisakhi. The day that holds the Khalsa's birth, the grief of Jallianwala Bagh, and the harvest, all at once. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Khalsa, the order Guru Gobind Singh founded at Vaisakhi.

carryVoice: Your line: birth, grief, harvest. All three can be true on one day. Back tomorrow, same hill.
